slides.title: Triangle Inequality Theorem; Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today: which three lengths make a triangle — and which make a right one.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q3 and Q4 are a pair: 6² + 8² = 100 = 10², today's converse before it has a name. Say that in one sentence after the reveal and no more. Silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Three sets of sticks on the longest one: 3 and 4 cannot reach across 9 (7 < 9); 4 and 5 reach exactly and lie flat on the 9 — no triangle (4 + 5 = 9); 5 and 6 meet above it (11 > 9). **Say:** add the two shorter sides — if that is MORE than the longest, it makes a triangle; equal lies flat. The FAST reference sheet prints all three inequalities; only the shorter pair can ever fail. It holds for every triangle, not only right ones (the state's named misconception, carried over from Pythagorean work). Real sticks or straws can fake the equal case into a 'triangle' — the rule decides, not the sticks.
OFF: 'Equal is not enough. Equal lies flat.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Two sides, 4 and 9. The third side has to be long enough to reach (more than 9 − 4 = 5) and short enough to be covered (less than 4 + 9 = 13). 5 and 13 themselves are the flat cases. Call the third side x and write it as one inequality, 5 < x < 13 — read it 'x is between 5 and 13'; the signs are <, never ≤, because 5 and 13 lie flat. **Say:** between the difference and the sum, never equal to either.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The 3-4-5 triangle with a square on each side: 9 + 16 = 25. That is the Pythagorean Theorem — memorize it; 6.03 uses it. Turned around it is the converse, today's test: take the two shorter sides and the longest; if their squares match, the corner is square. 24, 40, 32 is right (576 + 1,024 = 1,600) even though the longest side is listed in the middle; 5, 6, 8 is not (61 is not 64). Equal squares ⇒ right is the converse; unequal ⇒ not right is the theorem itself, since every right triangle's squares match — say both, because the book's keys lean on the converse for the 'no'.
OFF: 'Circle the longest side first. It is the only one that can be the hypotenuse.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: Can the three lengths make a triangle?
slides.note: Ask which two sides get added before anyone adds: the two shorter, 5 and 8.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 5 + 8 = 13, and 13 is less than 14: the two short sides cannot reach across. A board that added 8 + 14 and said yes tested the wrong pair — the only pair that can fail is the two shorter.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 7 + 9 = 16 > 15, so yes — a board that says no saw the big 15 and did not add.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask which side is c before anyone squares: 20, the longest, though it is listed first.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: The longest side is 20, listed first. 12² + 16² = 144 + 256 = 400 = 20², so the corner between the 12 and the 16 is square. A board that tested 20² + 12² against 16² put the longest side among the legs.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 64 + 121 = 185, not 196, so not right — a board that says 'right' added the sides, 8 + 11 = 19 > 14: the Triangle Inequality, not the converse (board 9).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).
